newsitem.title: USA: Clint Eastwood's ex-lover talks of humiliation.
newsitem.headline: Clint Eastwood's ex-lover talks of humiliation.

text.p: Clint Eastwood's ex-lover Sondra Locke testified on Thursday that she felt humiliated when she discovered the movie star had a secret deal with Warner Bros. that she alleges sabotaged her screen career.
"I felt annoyed, I felt embarrassed, I felt humiliated," Locke told a jurors hearing her civil suit against the man she lived with for 13 years.
"I felt horrible, I felt defeated," she said under questioning from her attorney Peggy Garrity as Eastwood looked on, sipping bottled water.

Locke, an actress who met Eastwood on the set of the 1975 movie "The Outlaw Josey Wales," alleges in her lawsuit that Eastwood undermined her contract with Warner Bros. Pictures to direct films for the studio.

"It is our contention that the deal with Warner Bros. was a sham," Garrity said in her opening argument on Wednesday. She said she would show that Eastwood secretly made a deal with the studio to reimburse it for any losses from Locke's films.

Her directorial efforts, "Ratboy" in 1986 and "Impulse" in 1989, were not commercial successes and in three years under the Warner Bros. contract, not one of her 30 suggested projects was ever developed into a film.
The case stems from Locke's original 1989 palimony lawsuit against Eastwood in which she claimed assets the couple accumulated during their relationship.

Locke later dropped the palimony suit when Eastwood agreed to secure the director's contract worth $1.5 million at Warner Bros. for her. But now Locke claims she was defrauded and is seeking damages of over $2.5 million.

Asked on Thursday if she knew of Eastwood's deal to reimburse Warner Bros., Locke said: "Absolutely not. It would have made no sense. It would have been like having an employer who's not really paying you."
According to court records, her lawsuit said Eastwood's action sent a message "to the film industry and the world at large ... that Locke was not to be taken seriously."
Under questioning on Thursday, Locke said she had earned nothing in 1994 or 1995 and only $10,000 this year for an independent film.
Eastwood's lawyer Raymond Fisher said the actor-director had no intent to defraud Locke and only made the deal with Warner Bros. to help her directorial career.

Eastwood, who rose to fame with a series of Westerns and the Dirty Harry detective movies, has more recently earned new acclaim as a director, including an Oscar for "Unforgiven." Locke was nominated for an Oscar for her first film role in "The Heart is a Lonely Hunter" in 1968.
